question: In a field trial evaluating a new nitrogen fertilizer on winter wheat, researchers record that 47 out of 210 plot-level subsamples exhibit root nodulation exceeding the target threshold. To account for the skew of the binomial distribution when the proportion is far from 0.5, they compute the lower bound of the 95 percent Wilson score confidence interval for the true population proportion. The Wilson lower bound is given by (2*n*p_hat + z^2 - z*sqrt(z^2 + 4*n*p_hat*(1-p_hat))) / (2*(n + z^2)), where n is the sample size, p_hat is the observed proportion, and z is the standard normal quantile for a two-sided 95 percent interval. cat(lower)

subtopic: when to use a nonparametric test
question: A psychology experiment measures reaction times in milliseconds for a memory task in two independent groups of 15 participants each. The distribution of reaction times in both groups is heavily right-skewed with several extreme outliers, and a log transformation fails to restore symmetry. The researcher wishes to compare the central tendency of the two groups. Which statement provides the most statistically sound justification for choosing a Mann-Whitney U test over an independent samples t-test in this scenario?
choices:
A. The t-test requires the raw data to be normally distributed in each group, whereas the Mann-Whitney U test makes no distributional assumptions and is always more powerful.
B. The t-test is invalid whenever sample sizes are below 30, while the Mann-Whitney U test relies on the central limit theorem to ensure accurate p-values for any sample size.
C. The Mann-Whitney U test is robust to violations of normality and outliers because it operates on ranks, whereas the t-test's Type I error rate and power can be severely compromised by heavy skewness and extreme values in small samples.
D. The Mann-Whitney U test directly compares group medians without any assumptions, while the t-test compares means and requires equal variances across all sample sizes.
